historic_survey.note: City Landmark No. 284, and the only one of the half-dozen suburban villas built in Duboce Triangle in the 1870s and early 1880s that survives with any of its original setting: an Italianate villa on a pair of adjoining lots, with an intact carriage house and a mature Victorian garden. The property has been reduced by a third from its original three lots. Christopher VerPlanck's context statement of 2022 surveyed 552 properties in Duboce Triangle for the Duboce Triangle Neighborhood Association. Dates it gives as “Ca.” are its own estimates.

historical_record.description: William Hollis, director of The Real Estate Associates and the city's largest merchant builder, bought the two blocks bounded by Castro, 15th, 16th and Noe streets, including this site; he later cut them with the new Henry and Beaver streets and sold the lots through the Hillside Tract Homestead Association from autumn 1868.
Built by Jacob Benedict, a silversmith and assayer, on lots in the Hillside Homestead Association tract.
Jacob Benedict signed the Spring Valley Water Company's water service application for the house, the earliest surviving record of it.
The house was first given a street number, 10 Beaver Street; it became 22 Beaver Street about 1895.
The Davis heirs sold the house for $4,000 to Mary E. Fee, a Market Street dry-goods merchant, who moved in and let rooms, the start of its use as a boarding house.
Two months before the 1906 earthquake the house was sold to Stephen D. and Emma W. Russell, whose family kept it until 1941.

Soon after buying the house the Russells added two bathrooms, one enclosed in a hipped-roof tower over the front porch, and built a rental cottage at the northeast corner of the lot (now 20 Beaver Street).
Stephen Russell took a permit, the earliest on file for the property, for the one-story garage built in front of the carriage house; it still stands.
With the Russell widow and daughter moved to the Marina, the house was let to the operator of a boarding house advertising meals by a German chef.
A $200 permit added a small room between the dining room and the back porch, almost certainly today's rear kitchen wing.
The easternmost 25 feet of the property, with the Russells' rental cottage, was split off and sold as a separate lot (now 20 Beaver Street).
An owner who had the lot rezoned for a hotel let the house to a tenant who sublet its rooms to young people from the Haight-Ashbury, leaving it a 'hippie crash pad'.
Photogrammetrist John S. Gieling bought the blighted house, which the city's chief building inspector had wanted demolished, and began restoring it.
The first restoration permit, estimated at $1,800, covered new kitchen and bathrooms, closets, code plumbing and wiring and a rear stair, to plans by architect Felix Rosenthal.
Red-tagged by the city in the late 1960s, then restored by its owners.
Architect Albert Lanier, husband of the artist Ruth Asawa, drew up the repairs required by a federal code-enforcement (FACE) inspection and plans converting the carriage house into a dwelling.
A dormer was added on the rear slope of the roof, the only notable exterior change of the restoration.
A certificate of occupancy was issued for the carriage house's conversion into a second dwelling, the work having been finished some years before.

hook: The Benedict-Gieling House, City Landmark No. 284 — the last Duboce Triangle villa left with its garden.

notable_residents.name: Jacob Benedict (c.1831–1887)
notable_residents.detail: Jacob Benedict, a Nova Scotia-born carpenter turned gold and silver refiner, lived here with his wife Ellen from about 1871 until his death on April 6, 1887.

notable_residents.name: George T. Davis (c.1830–1894)
notable_residents.detail: Wool merchant George T. Davis and his wife Abby bought the house from Jacob Benedict's widow and lived here until both died in December 1894.

notable_residents.name: Stephen D. Russell (1861–1917)
notable_residents.detail: Stephen D. Russell, First Assistant to San Francisco's Fire Chief, lived here until he was killed fighting a fire in 1917; his body lay in state at City Hall.

notable_residents.name: John S. Gieling (1925–1982)
notable_residents.detail: John S. Gieling, a Harvard-trained geologist and photogrammetrist for San Mateo engineering firms, lived here and restored the house until his death on October 25, 1982.
